cards.title: Choose Shopping vs Search by Buyer Type
cards.summary: Shopping captures most ecommerce leverage, but B2B-style bulk buyers on an ecommerce store often convert better through Search ads.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to split Google Ads budget between Shopping and Search when your store sells both to consumers and to businesses (bulk, wholesale, trade customers).
steps: Ask whether a meaningful share of your buyers purchase for a business reason: bulk quantities, trade/technician use, repeat supply, or known-supplier relationships.
Default to putting about 90% of ecommerce focus into Shopping, since that is where most consumer product discovery and greatest leverage sits.

Break that default when the store has a B2B component: B2B buyers tend to skip Shopping listings because shown unit prices feel wrong for the bulk deal they want, so they click Search ads instead. Example given: bulk eyelashes sold to technicians and small salons perform better on Search than Shopping.
If B2B applies, build Search campaigns around supplier-intent and bulk-intent language, and keep consumer Shopping running separately.
Segment B2B traffic and creative onto different landing pages so bulk pricing and trade terms aren't shown to consumer shoppers.
Judge by comparing cost per acquisition and revenue per click between the two channels in your own account rather than assuming the general rule applies.
caveats: The 90% Shopping figure is the source's rule of thumb for consumer ecommerce, not a benchmark for B2B-heavy stores.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Rebuild Google Shopping Product Titles for Keyword Reach
cards.summary: Structure Shopping feed titles around researched, converting search terms rather than internal product names, and generate variants from search term reports.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the Google Merchant Center feed so your product listings appear for more relevant search queries and earn more clicks.
steps: Pull the search term report and identify the query variants that already convert for that product type (for example 'formal dress', 'dissolvable creatine powder', 'clear', 'flavored', 'portable').
Move the brand name to the end of the title, or remove it entirely if nobody searches for your brand; the brand already appears lower in the Shopping listing.
Move the decorative or internal product name (for example 'Nathan dress') out of the prime position unless it is a recognised product name.
Lead with the highest-value relevant keyword plus product type so intent is clear to both the user and the algorithm.
Append as many relevant attributes as fit within the title character limit so you can be matched on more specific queries (for example colour or size attributes).
Continue adding researched keyword variants until the title is full.

If a product has variants (for example 50g, 100g, 500g packs) that each generate a separate Shopping listing, give each variant its own title, image and description aimed at a different keyword pool, even though they land on the same product page.
caveats: There is no golden title formula; base every change on your own historical search term data.
Roll title changes out gradually, not all at once; a bulk switch resets learning phases across campaigns.
This is a source-specific approach that should be validated against your own CTR and conversion results.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Diagnose and Break the Target ROAS Death Spiral
cards.summary: A target ROAS that keeps missing shrinks its own eligible audience until spend and conversions collapse, so reset the target aggressively when volume drops.
cards.use_when: Auditing a Google Ads account where spend has been gradually trailing off, or where target ROAS campaigns have stopped delivering volume.
steps: Look for the pattern over time: flat or rising spend, a dip in actual ROAS, then a steady decline in spend and conversions.

Understand the mechanism: the campaign stops hitting target ROAS, so it narrows the audience it bids on, which cuts conversions, which reduces the last 30-90 days of conversion data, which degrades the bidding model, causing a worse audience and further decline.
Recognise that seasonal dips, a strong product going out of stock, or any conversion drop can start the spiral through small sample sizes and worse targeting.
If you decide to lower the target ROAS, do it aggressively rather than in small steps; timid reductions commonly fail to arrest the decline.
Watch new accounts and recently onboarded campaigns for early signs so you can fix it before volume reaches zero.
Once volume recovers, avoid leaving target ROAS fixed permanently; rotate between restrictive and expansive strategies over longer periods to prevent over-siloing.
caveats: This is a mechanical failure pattern described by the source, not a universal rule; some campaigns with sufficient volume and stable history may hold a fixed target ROAS.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Pick Expansive vs Restrictive Bidding by Testing Appetite
cards.summary: Max conversion bidding spends ~30% of budget testing new audiences while target ROAS/CPA restrict auctions for efficiency, at the cost of siloing the account.
cards.use_when: Choosing or reviewing the bidding strategy for a Google Ads account and deciding whether you need scale discovery or tighter efficiency.
steps: Classify the strategy: maximize conversions and maximize conversion value are expansive because they can enter any auction; target CPA and target ROAS are restrictive because they only enter auctions that fit an efficiency target.

Use the rough concept that an expansive strategy allocates something like 30% of budget to testing new keywords, audiences, placements, regions and similar adjacent bets, which is what can unlock scale.

Assume a restrictive strategy has roughly 0% testing budget; how strict it really is depends on the gap between your achieved ROAS and the target. If you're hitting 4 and target is 4.5, testing is effectively zero; if you're hitting 5 and target is 2, it behaves more like max conversion value.

Weigh the trade-offs: expansive bidding wins auctions it otherwise wouldn't but also loses some it otherwise wouldn't, so it is higher risk; restrictive bidding is more efficient but silos you into one audience and demographic over time.
Rotate between the two over extended periods rather than staying on target ROAS permanently, to avoid a siloed negative feedback loop.
As a default for ecommerce, the source recommends going for value most of the time, because value bidding reflects product margin differences that pure conversion bidding ignores.
caveats: The 30% testing figure is an illustrative concept from the source, not a measured benchmark.
Bidding behaviour and available settings change; verify current strategy options in the Google Ads interface.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Maximize Conversion Value Instead of Conversions for Mixed-Margin Catalogs
cards.summary: Optimizing for conversions pushes spend to cheap products with low CPAs, so value-based bidding better reflects where the profitable orders actually are.
cards.use_when: Choosing between maximize conversions/target CPA and maximize conversion value/target ROAS when your catalog spans very different price points and margins.
steps: Model the failure case: a $40 t-shirt can acquire customers at, say, $20 CPA while a $200 jumper may cost $60 CPA, so a conversion-optimized campaign funnels nearly all budget into the t-shirt.
Check the ROAS of each: in the source example the t-shirt returns around 2x while the jumper returns around 3.5x, which is the outcome you'd prefer to fund.
Recognize that maximize conversions cannot distinguish these, because it optimizes for the lowest CPA and highest order count, not for value.
Switch ecommerce campaigns to value-based bidding (maximize conversion value or target ROAS) so the system weights higher-value orders.
Confirm your conversion tracking passes order value accurately before relying on value bidding, otherwise the model learns the wrong signal.
Review product-level spend after switching to verify budget is moving toward the higher-ROAS items you intended to fund.
caveats: The dollar figures are illustrative examples from the source, not ecommerce benchmarks.
Value bidding depends on accurate transaction value data; bad data will reinforce bad allocation.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Use Portfolio Bidding to Merge Learnings and Cap CPC
cards.summary: Account-level portfolio bid strategies let siloed campaigns share learning data and add max/min CPC limits on top of target ROAS or max value bidding.
cards.use_when: You have deliberately split campaigns into segments (brand, category, margin tiers) and want them to learn together, or you need to cap expensive clicks.
steps: Confirm you need the segmentation for a commercial reason, since the primary goal is still to have as few campaigns as possible.
Set up a portfolio bid strategy at the account level and apply it to the chosen campaigns so their conversion learnings are housed and modelled together rather than in isolation.

Use the portfolio to layer a maximum and minimum CPC on a target ROAS or maximize value strategy. Example: in high-end furniture where individual clicks can reach $10-$30, set a max CPC so the algorithm never buys a click above your profitable ceiling.
Treat this as the fix when too much segmentation has isolated campaigns from each other, since it recovers shared learning without rebuilding your structure.
Check whether the equivalent feature is available in your campaign types before designing a strategy around it; the source notes this capability differs by account tier and campaign type.
caveats: Portfolio bid strategies and CPC caps sit outside Pmax and Shopping in the source's account, so verify current availability in the Google Ads interface.
A max CPC cap restricts auctions, so set it from your own profitable spend ceiling rather than guessing low.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Exploit Search Campaign Smart Bidding Exploration
cards.summary: Search campaigns can use a smart bidding exploration setting that lets target ROAS bid outside its target in 10-30% bands to keep discovering new auctions.
cards.use_when: You run Search campaigns on target ROAS and want some of the scale benefits of expansive bidding without abandoning efficiency targets.
steps: Set the Search campaign to a restrictive strategy such as target ROAS as your efficiency baseline.
Enable the smart bidding exploration setting on the Search campaign so the algorithm can go outside the ROAS target in roughly 10-30% bands to test auctions it would otherwise skip.
Treat this as a middle ground between restrictive and expansive strategies, giving efficiency plus some discovery of new audiences.
Monitor whether the exploration produces incremental converting traffic or just erodes efficiency, and adjust the target accordingly.
Note that this option is not available on Pmax or Shopping in the source's experience, so it applies to Search only.
Verify the setting's current name and availability in the Google Ads interface, since platform settings change.
caveats: Source-specific recommendation; the setting may have moved, been renamed or changed scope.
Search campaigns are the source's secondary channel for most consumer ecommerce, so this tactic matters most where Search is already a focus.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Build Negative Keyword Discipline in the First 30 Days
cards.summary: Search campaigns need heavy negative keyword review early because broad targeting bleeds spend, then lighter ongoing management to avoid resetting learnings.
cards.use_when: Launching or taking over Search campaigns and controlling wasted spend on irrelevant queries.
steps: Expect the first 30 days to be the highest-leverage period for negative keywords, since campaigns go broad and pick up irrelevant terms.
Review negative keywords weekly in the first 30 days. If budgets are high, review daily to prevent keyword bleed and wasted spend.
From month one onward, drop the cadence to roughly weekly or nightly rather than constantly editing.
Avoid over-tweaking negatives, because every edit resets learnings and impacts performance.
Build a universal negative keyword list applied at account level so every new campaign inherits it automatically; search for an existing list, ask an LLM to draft one, or build your own.
Seed the list with clearly irrelevant themes such as jobs, careers, interns, hiring and salary, which should never receive your ads.
Use topic ad groups rather than keyword ad groups on the negative keyword side where you have thousands of SKUs; below that scale, this usually just overcomplicates the account.
caveats: The weekly/daily cadence depends on your budget level and search volume.
Exact negative keyword lists are not universal; audit yours against your catalog and business model.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Explain the Low Leverage of Average CPC
cards.summary: Average CPC is largely a vanity metric because traffic quality varies, so judge performance by conversion rate, AOV and ROAS instead.
cards.use_when: Reviewing Google Ads reporting or evaluating an agency's proposed CPC-focused optimization for your store.
steps: Write out the acquisition equation: cost per click drives traffic, and revenue equals conversion rate times average order value, so total return depends on all three.
Stop optimizing solely for the lowest CPC, since cheap clicks can be junk traffic that never converts and expensive clicks can be high-intent buyers.
Recognize that CPC and ROAS show very little relationship across large datasets, both at account and product level, in the source's analysis.
Keep only the peripheral extremes in mind: CPCs around $100 are almost certainly unprofitable, and CPCs around 10 cents are probably junk traffic.
Instead of chasing CPC, improve bidding quality by feeding the algorithm better conversion signals, quality score inputs and feed data so it bids on users likely to convert.
Measure success with ROAS and revenue per visitor rather than CPC movement.
caveats: The source presents this as a pattern observed across many accounts, not a formal benchmark; verify against your own account data.
This does not mean CPC is irrelevant in the extreme; extreme CPC levels still indicate a problem.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Win More Google Auctions by Raising Your Website's Conversion Rate
cards.summary: Because Google is an auction, a higher on-site conversion rate lets you afford higher bids than competitors and win more placements.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest to improve Google Ads performance when campaign settings have already been refined.
steps: Frame the auction logic: you and competitors bid on the same term, and whoever can pay the most wins the listing, the click and the conversion.
Accept that higher conversion rate is your lever to afford higher bids: if you convert twice as well as competitors, you can pay double per click and make the same money.
Apply the same logic to average order value: higher AOV extracts more revenue per click, so you can outbid competitors on the same traffic.
Use campaign structure, asset groups, audience signals and feed optimization to improve quality score so your bid effectively enters the auction lower than competitors'.
Recognize the counter-risk: a competitor with better conversion rate and AOV can outbid you even with worse ads and structure, so on-site performance ultimately caps what campaign work can achieve.
caveats: The doubled-conversion-rate example is an illustration of the auction mechanic, not a promise of results.
Without products and site improvements this advantage cannot be sustained.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Run Continuous Landing Page Split Tests on Search Ads
cards.summary: Duplicate ad groups with two ads pointing to two different landing pages, then rotate the winner against a new challenger every 30-60 days.
cards.use_when: Running Search campaigns and looking for the biggest lever beyond in-platform settings: improving the landing page conversion rate.
steps: Duplicate the ad in each ad group so ad one points to landing page one and ad two points to landing page two.
Keep the ads otherwise identical so the landing page is the variable under test.
Measure conversion rate over a 30-60 day period to give each page enough data.
Select the landing page with the higher conversion rate and make it the default.
Immediately start a new test: bring in landing page three as the challenger and compare it against the current winner.
Repeat the cycle so the campaign's average conversion rate rises over time, which raises the amount you can afford to bid.
Where possible, also test AOV improvements so revenue per visitor from the campaign rises alongside conversion rate.
caveats: The 30-60 day window is the source's guidance; lower-traffic ad groups may need longer or may not reach significance.
The source calls landing page testing one of the biggest levers in Search, but this is their opinion based on agency experience, not a measured benchmark.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Change Google Ads Budgets Slowly, Downward Faster
cards.summary: Google rewards slow methodical budget increases around 20%, and tolerates faster decreases, while other platforms allow quicker scaling.
cards.use_when: Scaling or pulling back spend on Google Ads campaigns after a winning period, or planning a promotion push.
steps: Increase Google Ads budgets in roughly 20% increments rather than doubling overnight; the source reports Google is a stable platform that responds badly to heavy budget changes.
Apply the same caution to bidding target changes: do not move target CPA or target ROAS overnight.
When reducing budgets from a high level, you can generally move faster with little instability or performance drop-off observed.
Treat other platforms differently: on Meta and TikTok you can increase budgets considerably faster than the Google 20% guideline.
Plan around the general principle that Google drives conversions consistently and wants slower, methodical changes, while other channels tolerate aggression.
caveats: The 20% increment is a widely repeated heuristic that the source confirms holds on Google specifically; it is not a calculated optimum.
Observed behaviour can change as the platform updates; validate on your own account.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Interpret 'Limited by Budget' as a Signal, Not a Rule
cards.summary: The limited-by-budget flag appears on almost every account regardless of spend level, so treat it as a hint to investigate incremental spend rather than proof it exists.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to raise campaign budgets when Google Ads reports campaigns are limited by budget.
steps: Read the flag as an indicator that the campaign could have entered more auctions if budget were available.

Do not treat it as proof that additional spend will be profitable; the source reports seeing it on nearly every account, even campaigns spending $5,000-$10,000 a day in a small total addressable market.
Investigate incremental spend by checking whether adding budget actually improves revenue and ROAS over a test period rather than accepting the flag at face value.
Combine the signal with other diagnostics: conversion volume trends, auction insights and marginal ROAS.
If incremental budget does not improve returns, leave the budget as is despite the flag.
caveats: Google's flag behaviour is the platform's own reporting and may change over time; verify current semantics.
Small total addressable markets can still show the flag even at very high spend, per the source's example.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Stagger Feed Title Rollouts to Protect Learning
cards.summary: Feed optimizations reset campaign learning, so roll title changes gradually and monitor CTR, CPC and returns in real time instead of switching everything at once.
cards.use_when: Applying Google Merchant Center title, image or attribute changes across a catalog with active Shopping and Pmax campaigns.
steps: Prioritize the highest-opportunity products or categories rather than the whole catalog at once.
Change a batch of titles, then watch campaign response before moving to the next batch.
Monitor click-through rate, CPC and return on spend for the changed listings in real time to see if the changes made a material difference.
Stop and redesign the keyword approach if results do not improve; test different researched keywords in titles instead.
Keep the baseline recorded so you can compare before and after the change.
Remember that a bulk switch resets learning phases on every campaign, which can put the account in a bad position.
caveats: There is no fixed batch size; pace depends on catalog size and campaign volume.
Feed changes can take time to propagate, so allow time before judging results.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Optimize Shopping Images for Contrast, Not Just CTR
cards.summary: Shopping images occupy about 70% of the listing, so design them to attract the right buyer through contrast with competitor listings rather than maximizing clicks from everyone.
cards.use_when: Improving Google Shopping listing creative to lift click quality, not just click volume.
steps: Recognize the image dominates the listing, with price and title as secondary click drivers, so image work is high leverage.
Aim for the right clicks rather than maximum CTR: if you attract the wrong people, higher CTR does not help, mirroring the idea that a headline should hook the right reader, not everyone.
Study the listings you appear beside and build contrast, for example keeping a photo shoot but changing the background colour if competitors all use white backgrounds.
Supply images in the ratio Google expects, about 4x5, and override feed images via a supplementary feed if your defaults, such as fashion's 9x6, get autocropped badly.
Where brand recognition is limited, focus on visual differentiation rather than brand-led creative.
Review click-through and conversion quality together after image changes to confirm you attracted buyers rather than browsers.
caveats: The 70% real estate figure and 4x5 ratio are stated by the source and platform defaults may change; verify current Merchant Center image requirements.
Higher CTR alone is not the goal; validate with conversion and return data.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Set Up Separate Merchant Center Feeds per Currency
cards.summary: Running multiple regions through one feed forces Google to show live currency conversions, which damages CTR and conversion rate.
cards.use_when: Selling to international customers through Google Shopping and reviewing your Merchant Center feed setup.
steps: Audit whether multiple countries or currencies are running through a single feed with one currency.
Create a separate feed for each different currency so listings display prices in the local currency.
Check how your current listings appear in each market; a live conversion label such as converted from AUD or USD plus tax signals a buyer that they are purchasing from an international store.
Fix the feed rather than relying on the platform's automatic conversion display, since that label suppresses clicks and conversions.
Review other basic feed attributes and descriptions at the same time, as this cleanup is largely a one-time setup.
caveats: The source frames this as a common audit finding, not a measured CTR benchmark.
Currency and localization requirements in Merchant Center change; verify current documentation before restructuring feeds.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Audit Responsive Search Ads for Learning Starvation
cards.summary: RSAs have 2,700 asset combinations, so heavy segmentation keeps them permanently in learning and you should minimise segmentation to let them exit.
cards.use_when: Structuring Search campaigns and RSAs for an account with limited impression volume.
steps: Note the arithmetic: a responsive search ad has roughly 2,700 possible asset combinations at setup.
Assume a very low 100 impressions to judge one combination, which still implies about 270,000 impressions to exit learning and know which combinations work.
Reduce segmentation accordingly, since every extra campaign and ad group fragments impressions and prolongs learning.
Work toward one campaign unless there is a genuine commercial reason, such as splitting brand from non-brand, for each added campaign.
Accept that in most accounts RSAs stay in learning indefinitely, and plan structure and expectations around that reality.
caveats: The 2,700 combinations and 100-impression assumption are the source's illustrative arithmetic; the source itself says 100 impressions is too little data to judge.
Low-volume accounts may never exit learning regardless of structure.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Follow a 90-Day Google Ads Implementation Sequence
cards.summary: Roll out tracking, structure, Pmax checks, waste audits, asset health and slow feed changes in a deliberate order over roughly 90 days.
cards.use_when: Onboarding a new Google Ads account or planning a quarter of work on an existing ecommerce account.
steps: Fix tracking first: ensure conversion events are firing correctly with no duplicate or stale tags, enhanced conversions and auto-tagging are on, and everything is up to standard.
Build a structure map: decide how many campaigns you need, starting from one and requiring a commercial reason for each addition, such as brand versus non-brand, and apply consistent naming.

Run a Pmax-specific check: asset groups split by product type, listing groups split out, brand exclusions on, audience signals present, and a target ROAS that is not so high the campaign functions only as retargeting.
Confirm the bidding strategy matches your intent using the expansive versus restrictive framework.
Audit for wasted spend: kill tiny campaigns that can be rolled up, add negatives for unprofitable search terms, and turn off display on Search campaigns if enabled.
Health-check ad assets: sitelinks, call ads, current promos, and maximise assets in every campaign to increase ad real estate.
Finish with a feed check on titles, images and remaining attributes, rolling changes out slowly rather than all at once.
caveats: The 90-day framing is the source's suggested rollout, not a fixed requirement; pace depends on account size and budget.
Specific settings and feature locations in Google Ads change frequently; verify each step in the current interface.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Exclude Brand Traffic and Use Smart Bidding on Search
cards.summary: Search campaigns should exclude brand terms and generally use a smart bidding strategy such as target ROAS or max conversions.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing Search campaigns in an ecommerce account.
steps: Set brand exclusions on Search campaigns so branded spend does not inflate Search performance.
Choose a smart bidding strategy such as target ROAS or max conversions rather than manual CPC or maximize clicks for established accounts.
Reserve manual CPC or maximize clicks for new accounts without conversion data, where smart bidding may not be available, and move off them as soon as possible.
Recognize that an agency may occasionally run maximize clicks as a deliberate arbitrage test, but this is rare and should not be the default for most accounts.
Review whether any Search campaign is entering branded auctions you did not intend, and correct the exclusion settings.
caveats: Smart bidding availability for new accounts depends on accumulated conversion data and may change over time.
Portfolio bid strategies can also carry brand exclusions and other settings; check where exclusions are applied.
The source works mainly with established businesses, so their default advice may not fit brand-new accounts.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx
